accroche: In 1794, a deputy coins a word to fight a practice. He will claim credit for it, without being quite the first.
contenu_vulgarise:
On 14 Fructidor, Year II (August 31, 1794), Abbé Henri Grégoire, a deputy in the National Convention, presents a report titled *Rapport sur les destructions opérées par le Vandalisme, et sur les moyens de le réprimer* (*Report on the Destruction Caused by Vandalism, and on the Means of Suppressing It*). The word that gives the text its title did not exist in French before Grégoire put it in writing. Two centuries later, it is still in use, far beyond the meaning it had then.

## A Word Coined Against a State Practice

Since the fall of the monarchy in August 1792, destruction has been mounting: royal statues melted down to make cannons, royal tombs desecrated at the basilica of Saint-Denis on the orders of the Committee of Public Safety, libraries and collections scattered in the name of the fight against the symbols of the Ancien Régime. Grégoire, who sits on the Committee of Public Instruction, opposes this destruction early on: he recounts, in his memoirs published after his death, having first been called a “fanatic” trying to save “trophies of superstition.” Only when the excesses become too massive to ignore does his voice find an audience in the committee, which at last agrees that he may present a report to the Convention.

In that report, Grégoire chooses a word that, until then, has no existence in French: he coins “vandalisme” from the Vandals, the Germanic people whose sack of Rome in 455 had made them, in European memory, the very symbol of barbaric and gratuitous destruction. The choice is no scholarly accident. Naming a practice by tying it to ancient barbarians disqualifies it in a single gesture, moving it out of the camp of the enlightened Revolution and sending it back to the obscurantism the Revolution claims to fight. Grégoire himself sums up the maneuver, years later, in a famous line: “I created the word to kill the thing.”

## A Word Older Than Its Self-Declared Inventor

History pushes back a little against the legend Grégoire builds about himself. The English word *vandal*, used figuratively to describe a destroyer ignorant of beauty, has been circulating across the Channel since at least the 17th century, well before Grégoire coins his French version. What Grégoire invents precisely is therefore not the idea of comparing a destroyer to a Vandal, but the French word *vandalisme* itself, endowed with a new political and administrative meaning: a category of offense that republican law can now name, and therefore punish.

The word did what its author hoped, and more. It left the vocabulary of the French Revolution to designate, today, any deliberate destruction of a good that belongs to no one in particular because it belongs, in a sense, to everyone, a graffito on a monument as much as a burned manuscript. Grégoire wanted to kill a practice by naming it; he mostly gave a name to a category that, for its part, never stopped existing.

carte.punch: He invents a word to kill a practice. The word outlived him; so did the practice.
carte.idee: In 1794, Abbé Grégoire coins the word “vandalisme” to fight revolutionary destruction, tying it to the ancient Vandals. “I created the word to kill the thing,” he will write, without being quite the first: the English word “vandal” had been circulating since the 17th century.

quiz.question: Why does Grégoire choose a word built on the Vandals specifically to describe revolutionary destruction?
choix: Because tying destruction to ancient Vandals disqualifies it in the eyes of the Revolution itself
Because the term already appeared in the revolutionary penal code and he only had to reuse it
Because the Vandals had themselves destroyed works of art in Rome in 1794, the year of the report
Because Robespierre, before his fall, had personally suggested the comparison to Grégoire
quiz.explication: Associating revolutionary destruction with ancient barbarians disqualifies it in a single gesture, in the eyes of the very people committing it in the name of the Revolution. No penal code already contained this word, the Vandals sacked Rome in 455 and not in 1794, and nothing links Robespierre to this choice.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How was Grégoire himself first treated, before finding an audience in the committee, when he opposed revolutionary destruction?
choix: As a “traitor to the nation” trying to protect the aristocracy
As a “fanatic” trying to save “trophies of superstition”
As a “conspirator” in the pay of foreign powers
As a “moderate” calling for the return of the monarchy
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Grégoire recounts in his memoirs having first been called a “fanatic” trying to save “trophies of superstition,” before his voice found an audience once the excesses had become too massive.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Was the French word “vandalisme,” coined by Grégoire in 1794, an entirely new word in its very idea of comparing a destroyer to the Vandals?
choix: No, the English word “vandal” was already circulating in that sense since the 17th century
Yes, no language had ever made this comparison before him
No, an identical Latin word already existed in Roman legal texts
Yes, but an equivalent German word had existed since the Middle Ages
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The English word “vandal,” used figuratively to describe a destroyer, had been circulating since at least the 17th century; Grégoire invents the French word, not the idea of the comparison.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What has been happening concretely in France since the fall of the monarchy in August 1792 that Grégoire's report aims to combat?
choix: Libraries are reopened to the public for the first time since Louis XIV
National museums are created to protect the royal collections
Royal statues are melted down to make cannons, royal tombs are desecrated
Ancient Roman monuments are restored exactly as they were by the new state
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Since 1792: royal statues melted into cannons, tombs desecrated at Saint-Denis on the orders of the Committee of Public Safety, libraries and collections scattered. These are the acts of destruction Grégoire's report aims to combat.
